speaker: Boaz Weinstein
title: Boaz Weinstein on the Money Stuff Podcast
question: In semi-liquid private credit or real estate funds, why can a standard 5% quarterly redemption cap still trap retail investors for years even when the fund honors every tender?
guest: Here is what I think overpromised is: in a large sell-off or in scenarios where there is a lot of fear, it is going to take you potentially years to get your money back. I might need to remodel my house, or my mother is getting old and I might need the money, and they say, "Well, look, for the last 20 quarters, you would have been able to get out of all of it because as long as it is under 5%, you are good. If it is 10%, and that is a lot, you can get out of half, five out of ten." But what happens if it is 40%? What happens if you are getting out of an eighth of it? And then of course what about reflexivity, a term that was overused in finance very long ago, but I think is very apropos here: the reflexivity of falling NAVs leading to larger outflows, leading to forced selling, leading to falling NAVs, and then you are out in three or four years. I don't believe that the retail investor understood that, and I wonder if it is even disclosed.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the cap applies to the whole fund, not to each investor. A fund that repurchases 5% of its shares or NAV every quarter is "honoring every tender" in the legal sense, but when requests exceed 5%, each investor is filled pro rata and gets only a fraction of what they asked for.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. If holders of 20% of the shares want out, each receives about a quarter of their request. The unfilled balance usually doesn't carry over automatically; it must be resubmitted next quarter, where it competes with new requests. Even if no one else joins the queue, clearing 20% of the fund at 5% per quarter takes a year; in a real run, rising requests shrink the proration factor further, so a full exit can stretch over several years. Investors also learn to over-tender to game proration, which worsens the queue.

Underlying this is a liquidity mismatch: loans and property can't be sold quickly without discounts, so the cap protects remaining holders and the manager's NAV. Boards may also reduce or suspend repurchases entirely, as non-traded REITs like BREIT and SREIT showed from 2022 onward.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
A 5% quarterly redemption cap applies to 5% of the *entire fund’s* net assets or shares, not an individual investor’s stake. In calm periods, few holders redeem, so sellers cash out in full. When sentiment turns and total requests exceed 5%, however, the fund fulfills tenders *pro rata*: if 25% of the fund seeks an exit, each redeemer receives only one-fifth of their request that quarter.

Once proration begins, crowding and compounding math stretch exits over years. Most funds lack a first-in, first-out queue, forcing investors to re-tender unfulfilled shares every quarter alongside new sellers. Seeing the cap bind also prompts holders who only wanted partial cash—or who fear falling behind—to tender 100% preemptively to maximize their pro-rata slice, swelling the backlog just as fresh inflows vanish. Worse, because the 5% cap resets against *remaining* shares rather than original fund size, payouts shrink geometrically as the fund contracts: if everyone tenders continuously, roughly 36% of each investor’s shares remain locked even after five years.

noweb.answer: A 5% quarterly cap applies to the fund’s current aggregate net asset value, not an investor’s initial stake, and oversubscribed tenders are filled pro rata without seniority for earlier requests. When sentiment turns, new inflows dry up while exit demands surge well past 5%. If holders of 25% of the fund tender at once, each receives only one-fifth of their request that quarter. Pro-rata rationing then sparks defensive over-tendering: investors needing only partial cash submit 100% of their shares to secure a meaningful payout, bloating the queue and pushing quarterly fills toward single-digit percentages. Because unfilled requests gain no queue priority, investors must re-tender their remaining balance every quarter alongside fresh sellers. Crucially, the 5% limit resets against a shrinking NAV, reduced by prior payouts and any asset markdowns, creating geometric decay rather than a linear 20%-a-year exit. In a fund-wide rush, redeeming 5% of the remaining pool each quarter still leaves over a third of an investor’s shares trapped after five years, even as the fund honors its full cap every period.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The 5% cap applies to the whole fund, not to each investor. It usually means 5% of NAV per quarter, sometimes 2% per month. When redemption requests exceed that limit, every requester gets the same fraction filled. If 25% of shareholders ask to leave, each gets roughly a fifth of their request paid, and the rest of the request is simply returned unfilled. The investor has to resubmit next quarter, and so does everyone else. The fund is technically "honoring every tender" up to the cap while most investors' money stays locked in.

The math makes it worse. Each quarter's 5% is taken from a smaller fund, so if half the investors want out, clearing the queue takes about three years. Because fills are pro-rata, investors have a reason to request more than they need, which makes the queue look bigger and stretches it out. Managers often sell their most liquid assets first, leaving the investors who stay with the harder-to-sell assets. New inflows, which normally fund redemptions, tend to dry up exactly when redemptions spike. Boards can also cut or suspend the limit.

BREIT is a real example: it limited redemptions from late 2022 into 2024.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: A 5% quarterly redemption cap limits total fund-level payouts, not each investor's exit, so when aggregate withdrawal requests exceed that threshold, every tender is filled pro rata. If investors collectively request 25% of net asset value, each person receives only one-fifth of what they asked to redeem. Because unsatisfied requests generally do not sit in a first-in, first-out queue, investors must resubmit their remaining shares each quarter and compete against both returning sellers and new ones. This creates a perverse feedback loop: anticipating proration, investors tender 100% of their holdings to maximize their slice, which swells total demand and drives the payout ratio even lower. Meanwhile, as net outflows and any markdowns shrink the fund's total asset base, the dollar value of the 5% cap shrinks with it. Even when the fund honors its full 5% limit every single quarter, receiving only a small fraction of a dwindling balance each period turns a full exit into a multi-year process.

If investors collectively ask to redeem more than 5% of outstanding shares, the fund can honor the tender by paying each investor a prorated share of the available amount. models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The 5% cap applies to the fund as a whole. If redemption requests exceed it, the fund can honor the tender offer by buying the full 5% it offered and still fill only part of each investor’s request. For example, if investors tender 25% of the fund’s shares and the fund buys back 5% pro rata, someone who asked to sell 100 shares sells only 20 that quarter.

The remaining 80 shares stay invested and exposed to losses. Depending on the fund’s terms, the investor may have to tender them again, with no priority over new requests. If demand stays high, each quarter’s payment can be a fraction of an ever-smaller remaining holding. Because the underlying loans or properties are hard to sell quickly and there may be no ready secondary market for the fund’s shares, quarterly offers give investors repeated chances to sell but no guaranteed exit date.
